title: The Four Categorical Statements
author: Study the Great Books
summary: This lesson from Study the Great Books's Foundations in Logic primer teaches the classical Aristotelian classification of all simple statements into exactly four categories, A (Universal Affirmative), E (Universal Negative), I (Particular Affirmative), and O (Particular Negative), each reducible to a standard form (All S is P, No S is P, Some S is P, Some S is not P). Rather than presenting the taxonomy abstractly, the lesson teaches a two-question diagnostic procedure, does the statement address the whole subject or only part of it, and does it affirm or deny the predicate, then applies that procedure to real sentences from Sherlock Holmes and Tolkien to show how ordinary language must be converted into standard categorical form before it can be classified. Its worked example on Tolkien's riddle line 'Not all those who wander are lost' walks through both diagnostic questions explicitly, identifying the qualifying phrase 'not all' as the textual signal that fixes the statement's quantity (particular) and quality (negative), yielding an O statement. The lesson explicitly positions this classification skill as a prerequisite for later lessons on the Square of Opposition and syllogistic reasoning, treating it as the first rung of a structured logic curriculum built from the trivium tradition rather than a stand-alone exercise.
points: Reduces the seemingly unlimited variety of possible statements to exactly four logical categories (A, E, I, O), each with a precise standard form, giving students a finite, checkable classification system rather than an open-ended interpretive exercise.

Teaches a concrete, repeatable two-question diagnostic procedure (whole subject or part; affirm or deny) rather than asking students to intuit a statement's logical category, making the skill explicitly transferable to any new sentence.

Uses real literary sentences (Sherlock Holmes, Tolkien, Beowulf, biblical text) rather than invented logic-textbook examples, embedding formal logic instruction directly inside the Great Books canon it is designed to accompany.

Fully worked example on Tolkien's 'Not all those who wander are lost' demonstrates the diagnostic procedure step by step, showing exactly how the phrase 'not all' textually signals particular quantity and negative quality to yield an O statement.

Explicitly sequences the lesson as scaffolding toward syllogistic reasoning, naming the Square of Opposition and syllogisms as the next steps, framing categorical-statement classification as a prerequisite skill rather than an end in itself.
quotes: Although statements differ in innumerable ways concerning their subjects and their predicates, making a nearly unlimited number of possible statements, it is nevertheless the case that there are ultimately only four categories into which all simple statements may fall.
A statements have, or are convertible to, the form of All S is P.

The process of converting statements into standard form starts with asking two simple questions: Does the statement address the whole of the subject, or just part of it? Does the statement affirm or deny something about the subject
In our sample statement the verb of being is have which is affirmative, so the statement is both universal in its quantity and affirmative in its quality and therefore is an A statement.

this statement clarifies this right at the outset when it qualifies the extent of the subject with the words Not all. In other words, less than all of the subject is related to the predicate, but also more than none of the subject is related to the predicate
Therefore, the line in consideration is an O statement, Particular Negative.

Knowing which category a statement belongs to is half the battle, but the other half of the battle is actually translating the original statement into Standard Categorical Form so that we may use it in a syllogism.
